_source.displaydescription:
Iku Bāhāḥ is one of the branches of Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440) and is located to the north-west of the main bāhāḥ. For this reason, this monastic building is also called ikuli or yakuli, meaning ‘north-west direction’. Nowadays, a family living in Mūladuvāḥ Kavaḥ (Nānicāyāḥ Kavaḥ) of Bu Bāhāḥ takes care of this branch.

Residential buildings surround the three-storey monastic building. The main entrance is flanked by a lion to the right and a śārdūla (leopard) to the left. Both of these statues were established in 1885 CE. The entrance to the sanctum is clad in brass and is surmounted by a copper repoussé toraṇa showing Akṣobhya in the middle with Prajñāpāramitā on his right and Lokeśvara on his left. An image of Padmapāṇi Bodhisattva has also been placed on the upper part of the toraṇa. The door to the shrine is flanked by small latticed windows, with a stone statue of Hanumān attached to the wall above the left window and an image of Gaṇeśa kept above the right window. On the left wall one can also find a stone statue of Mahākāla with three heads and four arms holding khaḍga, kartṛ, khaṭvāṅga and kapāla. The main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) is Padmapāṇi Bodhisattva. The façade of the first storey contains a latticed window flanked by two inscriptions and two smaller latticed windows, whilst the second storey has a large plain window. Historical photos of the bāhāḥ show that it once had a jhĩgaṭī-tiled roof. However, the building is currently under reconstruction. A dharmadhātu maṇḍala and a śikharakūṭa caitya have been erected in the courtyard.

In the 2015 earthquakes, a building standing to the right of the bāhāḥ collapsed and fell down, destroying two storeys of the bāhāḥ. This building was completely removed after the earthquake and is now under construction. The Lalitpur Municipality has provided 2.5 million rupees for its reconstruction. A photograph of the bāhāḥ complex taken circa 1974 (published in Pruscha 1975 C/P-47) shows that the ground floor of the bāhāḥ (as previously reconstructed) is similar to its current structure, with the exception that dāci apā (bricks) were used instead of mā apā (bricks) and the white plastered cornice was replaced with decorative bricks. The height of the first floor has been increased considerably (by approx. 50 cm) and the three old latticed windows were replaced with new ones of different sizes and proportions. A new carved brick cornice was added above them, matching the design of the ground floor cornice. The second floor now features a new wall made using dāci apā and a new window frame.

_source.displaydescription:
The Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and is part of a group of four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala, all of which are alligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the Caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.

Generally, caityas follow a pattern of placing statues of Akṣobhya to the east, Amoghasiddhi to the north, Amitābha to the west and Ratnasambhava to the south. However, within this Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya Vairocana is located to the east, Mañjuśrī to the north, Vajrasattva to the west and Amitābha to the south.

Gaṇeśa Phalcā 2 is located to the south of Gaṇeśa Mandira (SUN0102) and to the east of Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira (SUN0100). This one-storey RCC Phalcā is adjacent to the eastern entrance of the Bhṛṅgāreśvara temple complex. Before it was dismantled around 1986, the Phalcā had a gable roof with tiles. This roof was then replaced by a concrete slab supported by three RCC columns during its reconstruction. The rear brick masonry wall made from mud mortar and stones on the plinth are the only traces of the original structure that remain.

Dāphā Bhajana is performed inside the Phalcā, and so it is also known as Dāphā Phalcā. The monument finds most use during festivals.

_source.displaydescription:
Devarāja Bāhāḥ is located in Pyagaḥ Thā̃ to the east of the street that runs from Gāḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0510) to Pim Bāhāḥ Caitya (LAL0750). A somewhat hidden narrow door leads to the bāhāḥ’s courtyard, where a small shrine of Akṣobhya is attached to a six-storey building. The shrine has a small door surmounted by a toraṇa showing an image of Akṣobhya and flanked by latticed windows on either side. The structure has a two-tiered lime plaster roof with a towering bell-shaped pinnacle and a small stone caitya. Carved struts support the roof. In the courtyard, one can find a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya (140 cm high). Paved with brick tiles, the sunken courtyard measures 235 cm × 275 cm. A stone inscription attached to the left wall of the shrine mentions the date of its initial construction.

A member of Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440) called Devarāja Vajrācārya built this bāhāḥ in 1902, one year after he constructed the dharmadhātujinālaya caitya in the courtyard. It was worshipped daily and was a site for other religious activities to take place until the grandson of the founder, Dharmarāja Vajrācārya, passed away. The courtyard has since fallen into disuse and has become a dumping site for rubbish.

_source.displaydescription:
Yaṅga Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). This Bāhāḥ faces east, and its roof is tiled with jhĩgaṭī. While the shrine for the esoteric deity (āgaṃ) is located on the first floor, the sanctum (garbhagṛha) is on the ground floor. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is the bāhāḥ’s primary deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ). This stone statue lost its authenticity, since it has been painted in enamel paint. A Śikharakūṭa Caitya in the couirtyuard which was renovated in NS 1063 (1943 CE).

The bāhāḥ is mentioned in a palm-leaf manuscript from NS 159 (1039 CE). (Kölver & Śākya 1985, 103). The Bāhāḥ had been abandoned for a long time, and consequently turned into ruins. The local elders mentioned that it was haunted even during the daytime. Since it was not possible to run the daily operations of the Bāhāḥ, its saṅgha members, Yogaratna Śākya, Munirāja Śākya, Teja Bahādura Śākya, and others, handed over the Bāhāḥ to a Bhikṣu Saṅgha (an organization of some monks who practice at the Therāvāda school of Buddhism) in VS 2000 (1943 CE). Later in VS 2007 (1950 CE), it came under the jurisdiction of this organization (Śākya 2053, 3).

Following the hand over of the bāhāḥ, it was named after a Sri Lankan monk, Sumaṅgala Vihāra by Nārada Mahāsthavīra (Śākya 2053, 1). No one addresses henceforth the Bāhāḥ by its old name. Contemporary buildings surround the Bāhāḥ in the present-day, and it serves as a learning centre for the Therāvāda Buddhism.

Bare Nani is located to the south-east of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) in Bungmati. This nani is also referred to as a bāhāḥ (Locke 1985, 239) even though its architectural design does not much resemble this kind of structure. A pair of stone lions have been placed at its entrance, however the building lacks an āgãchẽ (a shrine of the esoteric clan deity) which is normally the main feature of a bāhāḥ. However, there is an āgãchẽ in one of the houses located at the south-eastern corner of the courtyard. Bare Nani is primarily related to the Śākyas who are priests in the Hayagrīva Mandira (BUN0002) living nearby. The saṅgha of the Śākyas is also active; for example, the initiation rituals of local Śākya boys are performed in this nani.

A vajradhātu caitya stands in the middle of the courtyard, and statues of the Four Buddhas have been placed around it with one at each of the four cardinal directions. The caitya has been covered with a thick lime paint that covers the motifs on the harmikā and trayodaśa-bhuvana. In front of the caitya, one can find a dharmadhātu maṇḍala and an Akṣobhya shrine, both of which were established in 1980.

Local residents claim that this caitya was established before the Red (Rāto) Matsyendranātha was brought to the Kathmandu Valley. However, there is no evidence to support this claim. The caitya was repaired in 1659, and the courtyard was paved with bricks in 1682. This year also saw two lion statues placed at the entrance of the courtyard. A parasol is offered to the caitya every year on the full moon days of Āśvina and Caitra. A feast is also organised on these dates.

_source.displaydescription:
There are many dabūs (traditional platforms) in the old settlements of Kathmandu Valley. Most of them were made in the Malla period and were used for the performances of dramas and dances. An inscription found in Nārāyaṇacaura, Naksal from the reign of King Jayadeva the second (713-733 CE) mentions two platforms known as ponḍimaṇḍapikā and prekṣaṇamaṇḍapikā (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, 569 and K. Tamot 2013, 20). In the Malla period, many dances and dramas were performed in dabūs, especially during festivals and ceremonies (K. Tamot 2013, 20).

Buṅgamatī's Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) collapsed in the devastating earthquakes of 2015. Fortunately, at that time the statue of Buṅgadyaḥ normally enshrined there was on a chariot travelling from Buṅgadyaḥ towards Patan and so remained unharmed. Since the restoration of the temple is likely to last many years, a temporary shrine building has been built on the foundation of this dabū to house the deity. This shrine building measures 412 × 412 cm and was built using regular brick in mud mortar. It is covered by a roof made of steel trusses, plywood and metal sheets. There were two large stone lions guarding the northern entrance and two smaller lions in front of the southern entrance of the Karuṇāmaya Temple. These have been moved to stand in front of the dabū. A bell suspended from a stone frame was also moved from its original location to the left of the shrine’s entrance.

Following the 2015 collapse of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) this temporary shrine was built to house the main deity of Buṅgadyaḥ (BUN0001-008). Also, two large stone lions (BUN0001-008), two small stone lions (BUN0001-009), and a bell suspended from a stone stand (BUN0001-010) were moved from the temple to the front of this temporary shrine.

No sources can be found with which to date the initial construction of this dabū. Every 12 years, two dances are performed here: jalapyākhã (a dance from Harisiddhi) and gathupyākhã (a dance from Thecho).
